Baalis
BAY-ah-lis
n. (a king of the Ammonites who sent Ishmael to assassinate Gedaliah; named once)
Hebrew Ba'alis, probably containing ba'al, lord or master; named once in Scripture, at Jeremiah 40:14.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · In the Text · Related

Biblical Definition

Baalis is named once, as the foreign king behind the murder that finished off the remnant left in Judah: “And said unto him, Dost thou certainly know that Baalis the king of the Ammonites hath sent Ishmael the son of Nethaniah to slay thee? But Gedaliah the son of Ahikam believed them not” (Jeremiah 40:14). His name probably carries the element ba'al, lord. The warning came from Johanan and the captains who had gathered to Gedaliah at Mizpah after Babylon appointed him governor over “men, and women, and children, and of the poor of the land, of them that were not carried away captive to Babylon” (Jeremiah 40:7). Johanan offered to deal with Ishmael quietly, and Gedaliah forbade him: “Thou shalt not do this thing: for thou speakest falsely of Ishmael” (Jeremiah 40:16). The warning was true. Ishmael killed Gedaliah at a meal, and the survivors fled into Egypt against Jeremiah's express word, which is where the book of Jeremiah leaves them. Ammon had been Israel's enemy since the judges, and the last blow Ammon struck was through a Jewish assassin, against the one arrangement that might have kept a remnant in the land.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Baalis is a biblical proper name and has no entry in Webster's dictionary of the English language.

expand to see more

Baalis is the name of a king of the Ammonites; Webster's 1828 dictionary treats common English words and does not define it.

It occurs once in the Authorized Version, at Jeremiah 40:14.

The Hebrew probably contains the element ba'al, lord or master.

He sent Ishmael the son of Nethaniah to slay Gedaliah.

Gedaliah refused to believe the warning and was murdered.

Key Scripture

Jer 40:14 — "And said unto him, Dost thou certainly know that Baalis the king of the Ammonites hath sent Ishmael the son of Nethaniah to slay thee? But Gedaliah the son of Ahikam believed them not."

Jer 40:7 — "Now when all the captains of the forces which were in the fields, even they and their men, heard that the king of Babylon had made Gedaliah the son of Ahikam governor in the land, and had committed unto him men, and women, and children, and of the poor of the land, of them that were not carried away captive to Babylon;"

Jer 40:16 — "But Gedaliah the son of Ahikam said unto Johanan the son of Kareah, Thou shalt not do this thing: for thou speakest falsely of Ishmael."

Jer 40:8 — "Then they came to Gedaliah to Mizpah, even Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and Johanan and Jonathan the sons of Kareah, and Seraiah the son of Tanhumeth, and the sons of Ephai the Netophathite, and Jezaniah the son of a Maachathite, they and their men."

Modern Corruption

Political violence is read as the working out of competing interests only, when Jeremiah names the foreign king who paid for it and the man who ignored the warning.

expand to see more

Scripture is specific about conspiracies. It names Baalis, it names his agent, it names the men who brought the warning, and it records the governor's refusal. The result was that the remnant went down into Egypt in direct defiance of the prophet, and the last chapters of Jeremiah are the record of it. God's providence governed the whole, and every man in it acted freely and answered for what he did.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's sovereign ordering of a nation's end leaves every conspirator and every negligent officer fully accountable for his own part.

Hebrew Ba'alis, probably containing ba'al, lord.

Named once in Scripture, at Jeremiah 40:14.

A king of the Ammonites after the fall of Jerusalem.

The warning given to Gedaliah was true and was disbelieved.
